concept.name: Estimator bias
concept.definition: The difference between the expected value of an estimator and the true value of the parameter it estimates. An estimator with zero bias is called unbiased; bias is an objective, long-run property of the estimation rule, not of any single estimate.
concept.intuition: It measures systematic error: if you repeated your estimation procedure on many fresh samples, would the average of the estimates land on the truth (unbiased) or consistently above/below it (biased)?
concept.mechanics: Bias(θ_hat) = E[θ_hat] - θ. Classic example: the sample variance with divisor n has expected value ((n-1)/n)*sigma^2, a downward bias removed by Bessel's correction (divisor n - 1). Bias combines with variance into mean squared error: MSE = bias^2 + variance, so a slightly biased estimator can be the better estimator overall.
concept.formula: Bias(θ_hat, θ) = E[θ_hat] - θ, where θ_hat is the estimator and θ the parameter; unbiased if this equals zero for all θ. MSE(θ_hat) = Bias^2 + Var(θ_hat).
concept.failure_modes: Unbiasedness is not preserved under nonlinear transformations: the square root of the unbiased sample variance is a biased estimator of the standard deviation. In finance, biases also enter through data selection - survivorship-biased fund samples make any return estimator upward biased regardless of its algebraic properties.
concept.misconceptions: Unbiased is not automatically better: a biased estimator with much lower variance can have lower mean squared error (e.g., shrinking variance estimates). Bias also says nothing about any single estimate - an unbiased estimator can be far off in your one sample.
concept.example: Estimating sigma^2 from n = 10 returns with the n-divisor gives E[S^2] = 0.9*sigma^2, a 10% downward bias; switching to the n - 1 divisor removes it, which is why s^2 = SS/(n-1) is standard.

citations.source: Wikipedia, 'Bias of an estimator' (citing Dekking 2005; DeGroot 1986)
